name: Back extension / deadlift strength

lead: Deadlifts and back extensions train the muscles along the back of the body: the spinal erectors, glutes, hamstrings, traps and lats. People use them to stand and sit more upright and to build a thicker, wider-looking back that reads as a broader, taller frame.

The deadlift lifts a weight from the floor to hip level and is one of the three powerlifting lifts. The back extension arches the spine back from a bent-forward position, bodyweight or loaded. The chain is stronger back and hip muscles, easier upright carriage, then a fuller frame. Both are standard strength exercises; no trial has tested them for posture appearance specifically.

paras: Deadlifts are done with a barbell or trap bar as part of a regular lifting routine, usually alongside rows and pulling work. Back extensions are done on a Roman chair, 45-degree bench or reverse-hyperextension machine, or with no equipment, often as a lighter accessory movement. Beginners typically start light and build load over weeks and months, with muscle and posture changes showing gradually as strength rises.

Rounding the back under heavy load is a common form error, described as controversial and a possible factor in injury. Trap-bar deadlifts are described as generally less taxing on the lower back, and back extension guidance advises lighter loads for beginners. Anyone with existing back problems may want to check with a clinician or coach first.

angle.text: Deadlifts and back extensions build the spinal erectors, glutes and upper back, which helps you stand and sit more upright and gives a fuller, wider-looking back. The path runs from a stronger posterior chain to easier upright carriage to a broader, taller-looking frame. They are standard strength training; posture appearance specifically has not been trialled.

lead: The deadlift is a strength exercise in which a weight is lifted from the ground to hip level and lowered again, most often with a barbell. It is one of the three powerlifting lifts and a signature strongman event.[1] The back extension, also called hyperextension, strengthens the erector spinae muscles through arching the spine back from a bent-forward position, performed on a Roman chair, 45-degree bench or reverse-hyperextension machine or with no equipment.[2]

Looksmaxxing and posture communities discuss both under the heading of posterior chain strength. Published encyclopedic sources describe the muscles worked and variations, but no clinical trial was identified testing these exercises for posture, back-muscle appearance or facial and body aesthetics.
infobox: Conventional, sumo, Romanian, trap bar; Roman chair, 45-degree, reverse hyper

paras: The conventional deadlift is described as working the gluteus maximus most, with the quadriceps, hamstrings, trapezius, latissimus dorsi and erector spinae also involved; the lumbar muscles contract isometrically to stabilise the spine during setup.[1] Variations include sumo, rack pulls, deficit, single-leg, trap-bar and stiff-leg deadlifts, and the Romanian deadlift, described as popularised by Romanian weightlifters and associated with posterior chain development.[1][3]

The back extension works the erector spinae. In the 90-degree Roman chair version the body lies horizontally for full range of motion, while the 45-degree bench gives a shorter range. The reverse hyperextension machine is described as also working the glutes and part of the hamstrings, and a 2019 biomechanical study in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research reportedly compared it with the standard hyperextension and found greater hip range of motion.[2]

Common deadlift errors listed include protracting the shoulders, letting the bar drift from the body, rounding the back and turning the lift into a squat. The article says whether back rounding is harmful is controversial and that excessive rounding may lead to injury, and describes the trap-bar variant as generally less taxing on the lower back.[1] For back extensions, the source's only explicit safety guidance is to start with lighter weights to avoid straining the back muscles.[2]

No studies found on these exercises as a looks or posture intervention. The biomechanics literature cited by encyclopedic sources concerns muscle activation and range of motion, not appearance outcomes.[2]
